idiom_name: Array/Dictionary/Set/String value types with stdlib copy-on-write; uniqueness check for custom storage
implementation_notes: Swift's standard collections are value types - the language documentation states that in Swift the standard collections Array, Dictionary and String are all value types - so assignment or parameter passing copies the wrapper while the runtime keeps one heap buffer behind a uniqueness check and duplicates the data only when a copy is actually written. Custom types reproduce this deliberately: a struct holds a class-backed storage object and each mutating method checks whether that storage is still uniquely referenced before writing, copying it first when it is shared. The refcounted handle is therefore already inside the language: model the value as a struct and let value semantics plus the uniqueness test do the work instead of writing a handle/body layer.
pitfalls: A struct with a reference-type property is only shallowly a value: the class instance is shared, and mutating it is visible through every copy.
The uniqueness check must run inside the mutating method on the struct - checking a copy of the reference says nothing about the storage about to be written.
Value semantics do not make concurrent mutation safe: share large arrays for reading only, or hand each writer its own copy / use an actor.
The first write after a share allocates and copies the whole buffer, so a hot append loop on a shared array copies repeatedly.
